en: The Ritual Manual for the Yoga Contemplation Wisdom of the King of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
in one fascicle.
Compiled by the Grand Master of the Household, Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, and Special Advancement.
I take refuge in Śākyamuni Buddha, who proclaimed the Mahāyāna sūtras of the Vaipulya and revealed them for the sake of all bodhisattvas—
this most profound, supreme, and true teaching. Now, relying upon this Great King of Teachings,
I shall explain the method for attaining enlightenment according to the Tathāgata Samantaprabhāsa.
If one can practice according to this ultimate truth, One will attain unsurpassed enlightenment in this very life.
Homage to the Introduction on Dependent Origination. Within the light, the matters of cause and effect are clearly revealed;
Virtue and wisdom reach their ultimate consummation. This is the gateway to the ultimate truth of the single vehicle’s true nature.
Homage to the Chapter on Skillful Means. The Tathāgata’s wisdom is profound and unfathomable;
Transcending the path of speech, it is free from the realms of mind and mental objects. Therefore, through skillful means, he teaches the Three Vehicles.
Homage to the Chapter on the Parable of the Burning House. Śāriputra was first granted the prophecy of Bodhi.
Sentient beings do not awaken to the suffering of the three realms; The Buddha, using the three vehicles as bait, entices them to emerge [from saṃsāra].

Taking refuge, they feel weary and remorseful; in this Chapter on Faith and Understanding, They feel deep shame for their own inferior vehicle, giving rise to a profound thirst and longing for that which is difficult to encounter. "We have all obtained the unsurpassed treasure."
Homage to the Chapter on Medicinal Herbs for Healing Illnesses.
The man born blind opens his eye of wisdom and attains the light of knowledge like the solar orb;
homage to the Chapter on Skillfulness in the Unsurpassed Vehicle. The four great śrāvakas receive their simultaneous prophecy.
Each has served various World-Honored Ones, and shall all realize the fruit of Bodhi in the future.
I take refuge in the Chapter on the Skillful Parable of the City of Transformation, wherein the Buddha earnestly explained the past causes and conditions:
he manifested a city of transformation to provide temporary rest, so that they might reach Great Nirvana as the ultimate goal.

Homage to the Chapter on the Five Hundred Disciples: The great assembly of Śrāvakas all receive their predictions, thereby awakening to the Tathāgatagarbha within themselves; they now realize the priceless jewel.
Homage to the Chapter on the Bestowal of Instruction upon Those Still Learning and Those Beyond Learning: The Buddha bestows his prediction upon Ānanda and Rāhula.
This demonstrates that the Dharma King has no partiality; He gradually gathers those of fixed and unfixed natures.
I take refuge in the Chapter on the Dharma Master Who Transmits the Sūtra.
If there are sentient beings in the future who uphold even a single verse of this Lotus Sūtra, The Buddha shall bestow upon them all the prediction of enlightenment.
Homage to the Chapter on the Stūpa of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna; The Manifestation of the Pure Land and the Gathering of All Buddhas;
Devadatta Receiving the Prediction of Buddhahood; The Dragon Girl Attaining Unsurpassed Enlightenment;
Homage to the Chapter on Exhorting the Retention of the Sūtra; Mahāprajāpatī and Yaśodharā Receiving Their Predictions.
May all the great Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas together vow that during the Dharma-ending age,
they shall encourage the upholding of this "Chapter on Reclining for Peaceful Practice" and its devoted cultivation. By preaching this sūtra while first abiding in peaceful practice,
one shall obtain extraordinary rewards in the present life and never regress from the Bodhi of the Buddha.
I take refuge in the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth. The Bodhisattvas of the eight Ganges-sands do not permit the Tathāgata’s secret intent to uphold this sutra;
In order to manifest the Bodhisattvas who have emerged, I take refuge in the "Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Lifespan," In which the Buddha attained enlightenment countless eons ago.
To subdue wayward sons, he manifests nirvana, yet he eternally dwells on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa without passing away.

I take refuge in this chapter on the Analysis of Merit. Having heard the Buddha proclaim his immeasurable lifespan, the countless bodhisattvas, as numerous as motes of dust, each transcended their respective stages and realized enlightenment.
Homage to the Chapter on Rejoicing in Merit:
If one hears even a single verse of this sutra, One surpasses all [other merits] and swiftly realizes the Unsurpassed Way.
Homage to the Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master: If one is able to receive and uphold this scripture...
In this present life, within the body born of one's parents, one attains supernormal powers and purifies the six sense faculties.

I take refuge in the Chapter on the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging. Through the practice of difficult and painful deeds in the past, hearing this sutra has increased his lifespan, and he brings immeasurable and boundless multitudes to liberation.
Homage to the Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Supernatural Power. The Buddha manifests the mark of the broad and long tongue;
he causes those who are hesitant and lack faith to attain pure faith. Seeing this auspicious sign, they attain the Buddha-way.
Homage to the Chapter on the Final Entrustment. The Tathāgata entrusts [the teaching] to all bodhisattvas.
In the future age of the final Dharma, one should circulate and proclaim this without stinginess;
I take refuge in the "Chapter on the Original Acts of Bhaiṣajyarāja.
For the sake of seeking the Dharma and the samādhi, he burned his own body as an offering to the Buddha Vimalacandra; this King of Sutras, difficult to encounter, manifests the utmost reverence.

Chapter on the Homage to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara: Coming from that buddha-field to this land to hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and having heard it in its entirety, returning to his own country;
homage to the Universal Gate Chapter of Avalokiteśvara, which explains the compassionate liberation of this bodhisattva.
It dispels all calamities and misfortunes; it manifests the eternally abiding, illusion-like samādhi.

Homage to this wondrous chapter of dhāraṇīs! It contains the mantras spoken by two bodhisattvas, two celestial kings, and rākṣasī women, for the purpose of protecting and upholding the Dharma-preachers of this sutra.

Homage to the Chapter on King Subhavyūha. Through the original causes and conditions of the two sages, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, as spiritual friends, one does not fall back from the path to bodhi.
Homage to the Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Exhortation. If there be anyone who [upholds] this Lotus Sūtra...
For twenty-one days, he single-mindedly practiced and maintained [the recitation], whereupon Samantabhadra manifested his pure Dharma-body for him,
as described in the Vaipulya Mahāyāna Sūtra:
"Within the bodies of all sentient beings..."
All possess the Buddha-nature and are endowed with the Tathāgatagarbha;
all sentient beings are none other than vessels for unsurpassed Bodhi.
If one wishes to accomplish such a dharma,
one must possess these four conditions:
first, to draw near to a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
A true spiritual friend is the consecrated ācārya.
Second is listening to the sublime Dharma.
Hearing the true Dharma refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the King of Sutras;
third is proper mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*).
Appropriate attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*) is itself the wisdom of yogic contemplation (*yoga-vipaśyanā-jñāna*).
Fourth is practice in accordance with the Dharma (*dharmānudharma-pratipatti*).
One who practices in accordance with the Dharma refers to one who cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā,
thereby becoming capable of realizing unsurpassed bodhi.
Whether male or female, those who practice and uphold the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* must rely upon the cultivation of mantras and practice the secret conduct of the bodhisattva path.
One should first enter the Great Mandala of the Matrix of Great Compassion and behold the homa altar,
thereby extinguishing the karmic obstructions within one's own body.
Having received the empowerment from the ācārya,
one should receive from the master the ritual procedures for recitation (*japa*),
as well as the samaya vows, the protection of the body, the delimitation of the boundary (*sīmābandha*), the invocation, and the offerings.
Even when contemplating one's own body as being identical to the body of the Great Bodhisattva Samantabhadra,
if one does not possess such superior conditions, [the realization will not be attained].
For all those who read, recite, and practice this king of sutras,
there is no means by which they can swiftly realize samādhi through each of the mudrās, ritual procedures, and mantras.
One should personally receive [the teachings] from an abhiṣeka-ācārya;
if one does not receive definitive discernment from a teacher, [it will not be attained].
If one acts with unilateral authority,
this is called transgressing the samaya for both the recipient and the bestower.
Both will incur grave offenses.
Once you have obtained the complete ritual methods,
you should immediately select a place for recitation and spiritual practice.
Whether in a monastery,
or in mountain forests, beneath trees, on rivers, islands,
or marshes, or in one's own house.
In a place of merit corresponding with the Dharma,
one should dig to a depth of two cubits and a width of four cubits, or six, eight, or even twelve cubits.
One should construct the maṇḍala at the designated site;
having excavated the ground,
if there should be tiles, rubble, ashes, bones, insects, charcoal, or any other impure substances [found therein].
It will then be unfit for use;
therefore, select a superior location, dig it out, and fill it back in.
If there is any soil remaining, it is an auspicious sign.
If there is any deficiency,
take earth from both banks of the river to fill it;
however, if it is naturally pure, that is most excellent.
Whether on a multi-storied pavilion, a flat rock, or a boat,
one need not discriminate when within a Buddha hall;
one should simply construct a mandala measuring four cubits.
It should measure up to twelve cubits (*hasta*) as previously described;
if it is twelve cubits wide, its height may be ten fingers (*aṅgula*) or twelve fingers.
In the northeast corner, it should be made slightly depressed.
This is a great auspiciousness;
it will be swiftly accomplished.
Once the maṇḍala has been completed:
In the center of it, dig a small pit.

Place therein the five kinds of jewels—gold, silver, pearl, musāragalva, and crystal—the five medicines—sahacara, bhaṇḍī, khaṭvāṅgī, nīlakaṇṭhī, and naulikā; if these medicines are unavailable, substitute them with the efficacious medicines produced in the Great Tang, such as *chijian* (red arrow), ginseng, *fuling* (poria), stone ginger, and *tiandong* (asparagus). Also place the five fragrances—agallochum, clove, saffron, *nālī* (camphor), and so forth—and the five grains—rice, barley, wheat, mung beans, and white mustard seeds. Thus, [place] these five jewels, fragrances, and medicines.
Take a small amount from each and place them together in a small glass bottle or a small ceramic jar.
Consecrate it one hundred and eight times with the Earth Goddess mantra. The mantra is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ pṛthivīye svāhā*. Furthermore, consecrate it one hundred and eight times with the Buddha’s Compassion mantra.
The mantra is: Oṃ buddhamaitrī vajra-ṭakki haṃ. Furthermore, empower [the object] one hundred and eight times with the mantra of the Vidyārāja Aparājita.
The mantra is: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānām, oṃ hulu hulu caṇḍāli māmeṣa svāhā*. Having thus performed the consecration, [one should proceed].
Place [the image] within the pit in the center of the mandala and fill it in until level.
Offer seasonal incense, flowers, food, and two *argha* vessels.
With these, he makes an offering.
The practitioner kneels for a long time facing the east,
pressing his right hand upon the place where the incense and medicinal herbs are placed.
Recite the verse addressed to the Earth Goddess three or seven times. The verse says:
O Goddess, you who provide close protection, For the Buddhas, the Teachers, who have practiced supreme conduct, Purify this ground for the sake of the perfection of generosity.
Just as the Lion of the Śākyas, the Savior of the World, defeated the hosts of Māra’s army,
so too shall I subdue Māra. Having drawn the maṇḍala,
I shall then take pure earth and cow dung that has not yet fallen to the ground.
Mix it with fine sand to form a paste and smear it upon the altar.
After it has dried, [proceed].
Furthermore, take *gomaya* mixed with scented water and smear it all over again; then,
pound lotus-seed grass and rub it across the surface of the altar.
While properly smearing, wiping, and polishing, recite the *bhūmiparigraha-mantra* for an unlimited number of times;
stop as soon as the smearing is finished. The mantra is as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānām. Aparājite jñānamati samatānugate prākṛtivīśuddhe dharmadhātuvīśodhani svāhā.* Having thus smeared the maṇḍala:
According to the dimensions of that mandala,
divide the positions of the deities and mark each with a dot.
Then, take threads of five colors and twist them together to form a cord.
Soak [the materials] overnight in a mixture of white powder, incense, and fragrant mud within a mandala; thereafter, delineate the mandala.
This mandala consists of three tiers.
Within the inner courtyard, draw an eight-petaled lotus flower;
upon the calyx of the flower, place a stūpa,
and within that stūpa—
Paint Śākyamuni Tathāgata and Prabhūtaratna Tathāgata seated together on the same throne;
the gate of the stupa opens to the west,
and upon an eight-petaled lotus flower.
Beginning from the northeast corner and proceeding clockwise,
one should arrange and install the eight great bodhisattvas.
First is Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Next were Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva,
Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva,
and Gadgadasvara Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Constantly Diligent,
the Bodhisattva Inexhaustible Intent,
and the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
As for Samantabhadra Bodhisattva,
within the four corners of this courtyard,
first, in the northeast corner:
Setting aside Mahākāśyapa,
next to the southeast is Subhūti,
and to the southwest is Śāriputra.
To the northwest was Mahāmaudgalyāyana;
next, in the second enclosure,
at its eastern gate.
Place the Bodhisattva Vajraśṛṅkhalā [at the western gate].
Place the Bodhisattva Vajraghaṇṭā at the southern gate,
directly in front of the main entrance of the stūpa.
The Bodhisattva Vajrāṅkuśa is at the northern gate, and the Bodhisattva Vajrapāśa is to the north of the eastern gate.
Having placed the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
place the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi to the south of the gate;
next, to the east of the southern gate.
Place the Bodhisattva Ratnaketu;
at the western gate, place the Bodhisattva Jyotirāja;
next, to the south of the western gate.
Setting aside the Bodhisattva Ratnacandra,
place the Bodhisattva Pūrṇacandra to the north of the gate;
next, to the west of the northern gate.
Setting aside the Bodhisattva Śūradatta,
place the Bodhisattva Sarvārthasiddhi at the eastern gate.
Furthermore, within the northeastern corner, [place him].
Place the Flower-Offering Bodhisattva;
in the southeast corner, place the Lamp-Offering Bodhisattva;
in the southwest corner, place the Incense-Offering Bodhisattva.
In the northwest corner, offer incense to the Bodhisattva.
Next, at the eastern gate of the third enclosure,
place the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
The Heavenly King Virūḍhaka is stationed at the southern gate;
the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa is stationed at the western gate;
and the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa is stationed at the northern gate.
To the north of the eastern gate,
place the Great Brahmā King;
to the south of the gate, place Śakra, Lord of Devas.
Next, place Maheśvara to the east of the southern gate,
and Nanda the Nāga King to the west of the gate.
Next, to the south of the western gate,
place the King of Kinnaras, Subhadharma; to the north of the gate, place the King of Gandharvas, Rūpaśobha.
Next, to the west of the northern gate,
place Rāhu, the Asura King;
to the east of the gate, place Māṇibhadra, the Garuḍa King.
In the northeast, place the noble Vajra Ucchuṣma;
in the southeast, place the noble Vajra Cunda;
in the southwest, place the noble Vajra Acala.
In the northwest, place the Noble Vajra Trailokyavijaya.
On the four sides of the maṇḍala, draw the boundary paths for food and drink,
and likewise draw the four gates.
A celestial canopy was spread over the mandala,
with twenty-four banners suspended from its four sides;
furthermore, a bannered pillar was erected at each of the four corners.
Place four auspicious vases with unblackened bottoms;
fill them completely with scented water,
and insert various seasonal flower branches within their openings.
On both sides of each of the four gates of the maṇḍala,
place two argha vessels,
filled to the brim with scented water.
Place saffron in the center and float various seasonal flowers upon it to make it exceedingly fragrant and pure.
Furthermore, place four incense burners at the four gates.
Burn incense of the five flavors to make offerings.
Furthermore, place copper lamp stands in each of the four corners.
Use clarified butter as the lamp.
Drive stakes of khadira wood at each of the four corners outside;
if this wood is unavailable, it is also permissible to use stakes fashioned from cast copper as a substitute.
If a practitioner seeks the purification of the six sense faculties,
fulfills six thousand merits,
and achieves the Lotus Samādhi.
Those who have entered the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) in this present life and resolutely seek to realize unsurpassed bodhi should,
for one week, three weeks, up to seven weeks, or for three months, [practice].
One should follow the ritual procedures according to one's capacity,
placing colored offerings, incense, and delicious foods on all four sides of the maṇḍala.
Various kinds of food and drink— milk, rice gruel, curd, rice,
sweet and crisp fruits, as well as various syrups; and offering articles such as unguents, powdered incense, seasonal flowers, burning incense, lamps, and candles.
One should use new, clean vessels made of gold, silver,
copper, or fine porcelain that are without cracks or leaks and have never been used before.
Place the food and drink therein,
and further use incense to fumigate the food vessels;
then employ the mantra of the Honored One, Ārya-Acalanātha.
Empower [the object] three or seven times.
The mantra is: *Namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa sphoṭaya hūṃ traṭ haṃ khaṃ*. Having thus performed the empowerment:
Thereafter, perform the offerings.
On the western side of the maṇḍala, one should place a low-legged stool at a height of about half an inch from the ground.
One should prepare a mat of pure *kuśa* grass and spread it upon that [seat].
This practitioner bathes four times daily and changes clothes four times.
If one is unable to do so at the appointed times, one should bathe separately at other times.
Thereupon, one should recite the purification mantra to consecrate the robes;
this is called the ultimate ritual bathing.
One should recite it three or seven times.
The mantra is:
Oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho ’ham. Having completed this empowerment, [the ritual proceeds].
He immediately entered the ritual arena (maṇḍala),
gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance as if facing the True Buddha in person;
with reverent prostration, he focused his mind with utmost sincerity upon the visualization.
Visualize prostrating before all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the entirety of empty space and the pervasive Dharma-realm.
Having completed the prostrations, place your right knee on the ground,
join your palms at your heart, close your eyes, and concentrate your mind.
Recite the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna* once.
With single-mindedness, direct your attention universally toward all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
You should contemplate with a concentrated mind the meaning of each and every phrase of the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna*.
Giving rise to great joy and the thought that such an encounter is difficult to find,
he immediately sat in the full lotus posture, formed the mudrā of meditative concentration,
and recited the "Chapter on the Lifespan of the Tathāgata."
Or they may simply contemplate the sublime meaning within this chapter,
with deep faith that the Tathāgata dwells eternally in the world,
accompanied by an immeasurable retinue of bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas.
Dwelling at Vulture Peak Mountain, he constantly preached the sublime Dharma with deep faith and without doubt.
Next, one should immediately recite the mantra of the Tathāgata of Infinite Life and Certainty seven times.
One should form this thought:
"May all sentient beings attain the immeasurable lifespan of the Tathāgata.
Having made this aspiration, one should then recite the mantra as follows:
*Namo ’parimitāyur-jñāna-viniścaya-rāja-tathāgatāya | Oṃ sarva-saṃskāra-pariśuddha-dharmate mahānaya-parivarte svāhā.* If a practitioner recites this six times every day, [the merit is immeasurable].
At that time, if one recites this mantra seven times individually,
it can extend one's lifespan, eliminate untimely death and determinate evil karma,
and attain physical and mental pliancy.
Free from all lethargy and indolence,
one will swiftly achieve accomplishment by upholding this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. Then,
using fragrant ointment— specifically white sandalwood and camphor ground with water to the consistency of mud— one should smear it over both hands.
Continue up to the arms and elbows.
Then, one should form the Samaya-mudrā of all Tathāgatas:
join the two hands in *añjali*, with the two thumbs held side by side, extended upward and upright.
It is accomplished immediately.
Resting the tip of the thumb upon the heart,
one enters the gateway of contemplation on the true mark of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The so-called seed-syllable *āḥ*, the heart-mantra of Vairocana Tathāgata,
resides within the lotus of one's own body-mind;
its color is pure white, like a conch shell or snow.
Luminous and translucent,
it gradually extends and spreads out to the measure of one cubit; then,
one should contemplate the gateway to the true meaning of this syllable.
The syllable A signifies that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen;
it is the self-nature and original source of all Buddha-dharmas,
and the fountainhead from which all verbal teachings of the pure dharma-realm flow forth.
All of these take this syllable as their root.
With decisive concentration and free from distraction,
one dwells in this visualization and then shifts the mudrā to touch the forehead.
Recite the mantra once. Next,
touch the right shoulder, the left shoulder, the heart, and the throat,
reciting it once for each.
When performing the mudrās of movement and reciting the mantras,
concentrate on a single object and perform the visualization as before.
Once the empowerment is complete, place the mudrā upon the crown of the head.
Thereupon, they disperse.
The mantra is: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānām, āsme trisame samaye svāhā*. By forming this mudrā and reciting this mantra, [the rite is concluded].
Then one beholds the stage of all Tathāgatas;
having transcended the paths of the triple world, one perfects the pāramitās of the stages.
Next, one should bind the mudrā of the arising of the Dharmadhātu.
Form the vajra-fists with both hands;
extend the two index fingers so that their sides touch each other, thereby forming the seal to be placed upon the crown of the head.
Within this seal, visualize the seed-syllable of the Dharma-realm.
The syllable RAṂ is brilliant white, radiating light everywhere that universally illuminates the entire realm of sentient beings.
One should be able to destroy the false afflictions of all sentient beings.
One should contemplate that oneself and all sentient beings are of one single dharma-realm, non-dual and without distinction.
Having performed this contemplation:
Then recite the mantra three or seven times. The mantra is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ dharmadhātu-svabhāvātmako ’haṃ*. While forming this mudrā, recite the mantra.
Then one realizes the boundless, pure *dharmadhātu*.
Next, bind the Vajrasattva Wheel-Turning Mudrā:
turn the two hands back-to-back, with the right hand pressing upon the left.
The eight fingers of the left and right hands hook with one another;
the left thumb enters the right palm,
and the right thumb is bent so that its tip touches [the others].
Place the mudrā upon the heart.
Furthermore, visualize that within the lunar disc of one's own heart is the syllable HŪṂ, white and pure.
One then transforms these syllables into the body of the Great Bodhisattva Dharmacakrapravartana.
Once the visualization and wisdom are perfected, one recites the mantra:
*Namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ vajratmakodhaka*. By the power of binding this mudrā and reciting this mantra while performing the visualization, [the result is achieved].
One is then able to turn the great wheel of Dharma for the entire realm of sentient beings.
Next, bind the Vajra Armor Mudrā:
join the two hands with palms hollowed and joined together.
Bend both index fingers and rest them against the upper joints of the middle fingers;
keep both thumbs upright and side by side.
Press the middle joint of the middle fingers together;
then touch the forehead with the seal and recite the mantra once.
Next, perform the empowerment once each upon the right shoulder, left shoulder, heart, and throat.
The mantra is as follows:
Namo samantavajrāṇāṃ vajrānkuśa hūṃ. By forming this mudrā and reciting this mantra, [the purpose is accomplished].
This is to don the adamantine armor of the great vow-decorations,
resplendent and brilliant,
such that all celestial Māras and those who create obstacles dare not oppress or intimidate.
At the time of correctly forming the mudrā, one should contemplate as follows:
"All sentient beings are submerged in the ocean of suffering of birth and death;
I shall deliver them all, so that each and every sentient being becomes no different from myself. Next, one forms the Great Compassion Mudrā of all Tathāgatas.
Interlace the two hands externally;
join the tips of the two thumbs and the two little fingers together,
and place them over the heart.
Having completed the mudrā,
one immediately enters the contemplation of the equality of the single characteristic and the selflessness of phenomena,
giving rise to a mind of great compassion that universally encompasses the entire realm of sentient beings.
"May every single sentient being attain the samādhi of loving-kindness.
Having performed this visualization, recite the mantra:
*Namo sarvatathāgatebhyo vidyādharibhyaḥ svāhā*.
Nasheṇi oṃ maṇivajre hṛḍṇaya vajre marase niya vidara bhaṇe haṇa haṇa vajragarbhe trāsaya trāsa.
Svāhā sarvamalāpahāriṇi hūṃ hūṃ saṃdhāra saṃdhāra buddhamaitryai sarvatathāgatavajrakalpadhiṣṭhitā svāhā.
Having formed this mudrā and recited the mantra, one enters the contemplation of objectless compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*).
This can cause [the light] to pervade the great trichiliocosm,
reaching down as far as the limit of the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*).
Like a vajra, immeasurable celestial Māras cannot shake it;
they all retreat and disperse.
If a practitioner performs this rite,
their site of practice becomes a city as firm and solid as vajra;
no obstructing spirits shall dare to disturb or afflict it.
May whatever aspirations the mind seeks be swiftly fulfilled.
Next, perform the mudrā for delimiting the boundaries of the directions and intermediate points:
join the two hands in *añjali*.
Bend the two index fingers and the two ring fingers so that their nails face one another,
and extend the two thumbs upright side by side.
Press the two index fingers together;
by separating the two little fingers, the seal is formed.
Rotate this seal three times clockwise.
This immediately constitutes the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*). The mantra is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ, le lu-bhūri-vikule vikule svāhā*. Next, [employ] the mudrā and mantra of the Noble Acala.
To dispel all evil māras and obstacles,
hold the right hand upright with the index and middle fingers joined together.
The ring finger and little finger are bent into the palm;
the thumb presses upon the nails of the ring and little fingers.
The left hand is done in the same manner.
Place the left hand at the heart as the scabbard;
place the right hand as the sword within that scabbard.
Recite the mantra, and then perform the gesture of drawing the sword.
Rotate the mudrā counter-clockwise to dispel obstacles and difficulties;
rotate the mudrā clockwise to establish a boundary at whatever distance one desires.
At the time of binding the mudrā:
One should contemplate oneself as this very deity,
holding a vajra-noose in the left hand and a vajra-wisdom sword in the right hand.
The majestic power and radiance pervade the entire *dharmadhātu*.
Having performed this visualization, one recites the mantra:
*Namaḥ samantavajrāṇāṃ caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa sphoṭaya hūṃ traṭ haṃ khaṃ*. By forming this mudrā and remaining in this contemplative practice while reciting the mantra, [the result is attained].
It can protect the bodhicitta and sever all views;
if a practitioner constantly maintains this mantra, [these benefits will be attained].
Until they reach enlightenment,
they will no longer be susceptible to the influence of Māras and will swiftly attain perfect awakening.
Next, one should bind the Jewel Mountain mudrā and recite the Jewel Mountain mantra.
Interlace the two hands with the palms facing inward, drawing them together very tightly so that the two elbows touch; then extend the wrists. This is it.
The mantra is: Oṃ ajara hūṃ. By forming this mudrā and reciting the mantra, through its power of empowerment, this very mountain of jewels [is transformed].
Within that maṇḍala, it transforms into Vulture Peak Mountain;
upon the mountain peak,
one should focus the mind with single-minded concentration.
Visualize the place where the Tathāgata Śākyamuni proclaims the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
the ground is made of crystal,
and various exquisite flowers are strewn everywhere upon it.
Rows of jewel trees are in full bloom with precious flowers;
from their branches hang exquisite celestial garments, which,
when stirred by a gentle breeze, produce subtle and wondrous sounds.
The sound is harmonious and resonant, like celestial music.
A wondrous fragrance pervasively perfumes the trichiliocosm.
Furthermore, within that space, one should visualize the precious stupa containing the relics of the World-Honored One, Prabhūtaratna.
Adorned with various ornaments,
Śākyamuni Tathāgata and Prabhūtaratna Buddha sat together upon a single seat within that stupa.
An immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings, as well as other holy ones,
surrounded him on all eight sides to listen to the Dharma.
There were also the various emanation-buddhas of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
Beneath each of the jewel trees, they sat individually upon lion thrones adorned with various jewels.
This continued until there were Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of infinite worlds;
before each of these Many-Treasure Stūpas, the *bhadra-ghaṭa* and *argha* vessels were filled to the brim with water possessing the eight virtues.
Exquisite jewel incense burners burned priceless incense;
mani-jewel kings served as lamps and candles;
and wonderful bodhi flowers were scattered everywhere before all the Buddhas and the great assembly.
The various celestial delicacies were fragrant and pure;
clouds and oceans of offerings consisting of unguents, powdered incense, pearl garlands,
and necklaces made offerings to the Bodhisattva through the various pāramitās.
They praised the Tathāgata’s true merits with songs,
and they saw themselves making offerings therein throughout the eight directions.
Before each of the emanated Buddhas,
one likewise makes such offerings and presents.
Furthermore, one visualizes oneself before Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
Having heard the proclamation of the supreme meaning of the Mahāyāna *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*,
and having made this contemplation, one should recite this verse:
By the power of my merit, And by the power of the Tathāgata’s empowerment...
And by the power of the Dharma-realm, one universally makes offerings and dwells [therein].
Recite this verse three or seven times.
Then, recite the Great Ākāśagarbha Universal Offering Mantra, which says:
"Oṃ gaganasvabhāva vajra hūṃ. By reciting this verse and this mantra, [one makes offerings] to all the Tathāgatas and the great assembly.
All shall receive true and vast offerings.
Next, one should contemplate the assembly of the three-tiered maṇḍala:
first, the central Buddha together with the eight great bodhisattvas and the four great śrāvaka monks.
In the second court are immeasurable and innumerable bodhisattvas;
in the third court are the various devas and the eight classes of beings, along with the four great majestic bodhisattvas,
each situated at one of the four corners.
Together with an immeasurable retinue of wrathful deities,
they cause all māras to retreat and disperse so that none may cause further disturbance. Then,
one forms the seal of the Bodhisattva Who Turns the Wheel of Dharma upon the Mere Arising of Thought.
Form the vajra-fists with both hands;
interlace the two index fingers and the two little fingers with one another,
and it is accomplished.
Press the mudrā upon the maṇḍala and recite the mantra five times. The mantra is:
Oṃ vajracakra hūṃ jaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ jūḥ. By forming this mudrā and reciting this mantra, [the purpose is accomplished].
Within that maṇḍala, the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and all the assembly of holy ones are as vast as space,
pervading the entire Dharma-realm, forming a Buddha-field of the reward land for all sentient beings.
With body and mind profoundly unified in a single characteristic,
one manifests as a reflection within this supreme and wondrous realm;
thereupon, one should enter the contemplative practice of the Dharma-nature of True Suchness at the site of enlightenment.
Then, recite this verse and contemplate its true, ultimate meaning until the mind accords with the essential nature of *tathatā* (suchness). The verse says:
"Space is the site of enlightenment; Bodhi has the characteristic of space."
Nor is there any who attains equal enlightenment, for suchness is the Tathāgata.
Next, he binds the seal for inviting all Tathāgatas and the assembly of noble ones:
interlace the two hands with the palms facing inward and form fists.
Extend the index finger of the right hand and bend its upper joint like a hook;
this constitutes the true mantra, which is as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānām. Aḥ sarvatrāpratihatatathāgataguhyamudrācaryāparivāraka svāhā.* By forming this mudrā and reciting this mantra, [the rite is accomplished].
All the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, together with their retinues,
gathered there without exception;
the practitioner saw them clearly and distinctly dwelling in the air atop Vulture Peak Mountain.
Then, take the arghya vessel from the right side;

holding it with both hands at the level of the forehead, offer it while visualizing that the feet of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the assembly of noble ones are being bathed. This arghya vessel may be made of gold, silver, refined copper, agate, or conch shell.
Such vessels as these should all conform to the Dharma; select any one type and fill it completely with pure, wondrously fragrant, and clean water,
upon which float seasonal flowers.
Add a small amount of saffron as well.
When first inviting [the deities], take those from the right side;

when sending them off, use those from the left side. At that time, with utmost reverence and solemnity, address the Buddhas and pray for the fulfillment of your heart’s desire. The mantra is as follows:
Namo samanta-buddhānām. Āgaccha samayasamaya svāhā. By means of this offering of *argha* perfumed water, may the three karmas of the practitioner be purified.
Wash away all afflictions, transgressions, and defilements.
Next, one should form the mudrā for offering the flower seat:
the thumbs and little fingers of both hands should be joined tip-to-tip on their respective sides.
When one wishes to arrange the remaining six fingers in the shape of a lotus, the mantra is as follows:
*Namo samantabuddhānām oṃ yūḥ*. By the power of binding this mudrā and reciting this mantra with empowerment, [the purpose is accomplished].
From this mudrā, there immediately flow forth immeasurable precious lion thrones, lotus thrones, and various other seats for the Buddha,
the bodhisattvas, and all the assembly of noble ones.
Each shall obtain a sublime seat according to what is appropriate for them.
Next, form the general mudrā by interlacing the two hands with the palms facing inward to form fists.
Cause the joints of the fingers to rise slightly,
and then recite the mantras of Bhaisajyaraja Bodhisattva and others as follows:

*Tadyathā | iddime | iddime | iddime | iddime | iddime | nime | nime | nime | nime | nime | ruhe | ruhe | ruhe | ruhe | ruhe | sādho | sādho | sādho | sādho | sādho | svāhā.* Because one recites the various mantras as above, [the following occurs].
They will bestow great empowerment upon those who uphold this sutra;
all evil spirits and ghosts will keep their distance and dare not approach them.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—even in dreams—they shall not dare to disturb or harass them.
At all times, one shall obtain peace and happiness;
one should reflect in this way upon this King of Sutras, the Lotus Sutra.
They give rise to a heart of profound reverence and the thought that such an encounter is difficult to find;
they further reflect, saying:
"From beginningless birth and death..."
Cycling through the six realms of rebirth is entirely due to false, inverted discrimination;
thus, one fails to encounter early on such a sovereign teaching, the Dharma of the Bodhisattva path.
That we have now been able to hear, see, receive, uphold, read,
and recite it is entirely due to the compassionate pity of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
who have caused us to encounter such a wondrous Dharma, this King of Sutras.
How can such profound kindness be repaid?
Even if the three thousandfold world system were filled with every kind of exquisite treasure, as well as food, drink, incense, and flowers;
Banners, canopies, kingdoms, cities, wives, and children—
as numerous as motes of dust— and even his own body and life,
he likewise gave away entirely in alms.
Even if one were to make offerings to the Tathāgata and this precious Mahāyāna Dharma of the Lotus Sutra for many eons,
one would still be unable to repay the debt of gratitude for even a single verse.
Deeply feeling shame and remorse,
he further thought to himself:
"As I have heard..."
The Tathāgata Samantaprabha proclaimed for the sake of the bodhisattvas the secret dharma of mantra offerings;
among all the offerings in the world, this is supreme.
The offering of the Dharma is the most supreme and excellent.
Now, in order to repay the profound kindness of all Buddhas,
I shall rely upon the ritual manual of the bodhisattva’s skillful means for the practice of mantra.

Having made this thought, "I universally offer these to all Buddhas and great Bodhisattvas throughout the entirety of space and the Dharma-realm," one should then form the mudrā of the scented ointment.
First, extend the right hand with the palm facing outward.
Grasp the right wrist with the left hand;
this constitutes the mudrā of the gesture of applying fragrant unguents.
The mantra is: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ viśuddha-jñāna-āvahāya svāhā*. While reciting this mantra, one should perform the hand gesture (*mudrā*).
Visualize that from the inconceivable power of the blessings and vows of the mudrās and mantras,
immeasurable and boundless clouds and oceans of scented ointments flow forth,
universally anointing the pure and wondrous physical bodies of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and holy assemblies, as well as their buddha-fields.
By performing this rite,

one obtains the fragrance of the Dharma-body consisting of the five untainted aggregates— ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation— in both the present and future lives. Should one, however,
transgress the code of ethical discipline within the Vinaya of the Śrāvaka vehicle, [the following applies].
Should one violate the pure ethical discipline within the Bodhisattva path,
by merely forming this mudrā and reciting the mantra once,
all categories of precepts will become completely pure as before.
One will not fall into the evil realms and will swiftly realize samādhi.
Next, form the mudrā for offering flowers:
interlace the two hands with the palms facing inward.
The two index fingers are joined together to form a circle.
The two thumbs each press against the base of the index fingers.
The remaining six fingers are tucked into the palms.
To form the shape of a flower is as follows. The mantra is:
*Oṃ sarvabuddhānāṃ mahāmaitry-abhyudgate svāhā*. While correctly forming the mudrā and reciting the mantra, [one should visualize it].
Visualize with focused contemplation:
from within this dharma of the inconceivable power of the empowerment of the seal, mantra, and vow,
there flow forth infinite and boundless clouds of exquisite celestial flowers.
One makes offerings to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the assembly of noble ones.
By binding this mudrā and reciting this mantra,
one is able to cause the lotus of one's own mind to blossom.
The six sense faculties are purified;
they attain the marks and signs of physical excellence, becoming upright and majestic, such that all people delight in beholding them.
Regarding all afflictions and secondary afflictions...
Unstained by defilements, with body and mind tranquil,
next perform the mudrā of offering incense.
With both hands, join the three fingers from the middle finger downward.
The two middle fingers are held back-to-back.
The two index fingers are placed side-by-side against each other.
Each of the two thumbs presses down at the base of its respective index finger.
It is then accomplished. The mantra is:
*Namaḥ samantabuddhānāṃ dharmadhātvanugate svāhā*. While binding this mudrā and reciting the mantra, [one should do so].
Visualize with a focused mind:
from within the empowerment of the inconceivable power of the vows of the mudrā and mantra,
there flow forth immeasurable and boundless oceans of clouds of burning incense.
It universally perfumes all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the assembly of noble ones.
By forming this mudrā and reciting the mantra,
one attains the Prajñāpāramitā.
One will be able to sever all evil views along with all fetters and latent tendencies,
and swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Next, perform the seal for the offering of food and drink.
With both hands joined with palms hollowed, open the palms so that they resemble the shape of a vessel;
this is the mantra: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānām, arara karara marinda ni mahamari svāhā*. While correctly forming this mudrā, recite the mantra.
With utmost sincerity, one should direct the visualization:
from within the empowerment of the inconceivable power of the mudrās, mantras, and wondrous vows,
there flow forth infinite and boundless clouds and oceans of sublime celestial fragrances and pure offerings of food and drink.
Before each of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and noble assemblies,
one arranges and presents offerings using vessels made of the seven precious gems;
by forming this mudrā and reciting the mantra, one performs mental worship.
One obtains the food of the joy of Dharma, the food of the delight in dhyāna, and the supreme flavor of the food of liberation.
Next, form the mudrā for offering the lamp-light:
make a fist with the right hand.
Straighten the middle finger upward and form the mudrā;
then recite the mantra: *Namo samantabuddhānāṃ tathāgatājñāspharaṇavāsana-gaganodariye svāhā*. While binding this mudrā, recite the mantra.
Focus the mind and contemplate with clarity:
from the inconceivable power of the empowerment of the seals, mantras, and vows of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
there flow forth immeasurable and boundless clouds and oceans of light, like kings of various jewels, and like the radiance of the sun, moon, lamps, and candles.
It illuminates all the great assemblies of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
By binding this mudrā and reciting this mantra,
one attains the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*).
This can extinguish the afflictions of the ground of abiding ignorance.
Having performed this offering, the practitioner next enters the samādhi of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
One contemplates all phenomena as being like illusions because they arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions;
through the skillful means of realizing that all sentient beings are ungraspable,
one contemplates all phenomena as being like mirages.
From the supreme Pure and Wondrous Buddha-field above,
down to the defiled worlds below,
there is likewise nothing to be apprehended, taking this as the skillful means.
One contemplates all phenomena as being like a dream;
regarding worldly enjoyments,
one employs the skillful means of knowing that both pleasant and painful sensations are ultimately unapprehendable.
One contemplates all phenomena as being like reflections;
taking the non-apprehension of the karmic actions of oneself and others as the skillful means,
one contemplates all phenomena as being like echoes.
One knows all the verbal activities of oneself and others,
from the Buddhas above down to all classes of sentient beings below,
by means of the expedient of non-apprehension.
One contemplates all phenomena as being like shadows and reflections.
Regarding the minds of oneself and others, one knows that the mind and its mental factors are neither identical nor separate,
employing the realization of total non-apprehension as the skillful means.
They immediately realize suchness and contemplate all phenomena as being like the moon reflected in water—
bodhisattvas from the first stage up to the Dharma-cloud stage.
Contemplate the mind as being like water;
contemplate the samādhi of the pure bodhicitta as being like the moon.
The mind and the moon are non-dual and without distinction.
Furthermore, taking non-apprehension as the skillful means,
one realizes suchness and contemplates all phenomena as being like the emanations of a Buddha.
Knowing that the mind and mental factors take objects as their focus,
one enters the samādhi of great emptiness by employing non-apprehension as the means.
The *tathatā* dharmadhātu pervades the Buddha-realm and the realm of sentient beings;
it is without interval or interruption, transcends verbal expression,
and is free from the subject-object duality of the perceiver and the perceived.
If one approaches this from the perspective of true realization,
it is attained solely within the sphere of the noble wisdom of self-awakening;
next, one should immediately bind the samādhi-mudrā.
Form the double-vajra-bind (vajrabandha) with both hands facing upward upon the crossed legs;
bend the middle joints of the two index fingers so that their nails touch and their backs are joined.
Place the tips of the two thumbs against each other at the tips of the index fingers and position them below the navel.
Close the eyes, clarify the mind, and recite the mantra for penetrating and unobstructed mind seven times, saying:
*Oṃ jita-prativedhaṃ karomi*. Having recited the mantra, one should then meditate with focused concentration.
One seeks one's own mind:
"Now, as for this mind of mine,
is it blue, yellow, red, or white?"
Is it square, round, long, or short?
Is it of the past, of the future, or is it of the present?
After searching for a long while, one finally realizes that this mind is ultimately ungraspable;
thus, one can penetrate the contemplation of emptiness,
wherein both the grasping at a self and the grasping at phenomena are likewise ungraspable.
Thus one is able to awaken to and enter the wisdom of the emptiness of persons and the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena;
then, within this mind of non-apprehension,
one contemplates perfect luminosity.
Pure and free from dust or obscuration like the full moon in autumn,
it manifests radiantly upon the body and above the heart;
this is the primordial source, the pure Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
Having performed this visualization, one should recite the Bodhicitta mantra seven times.
The mantra is: Oṃ bodhicittam utpādayāmi. Having recited the mantra, [one proceeds].
Upon the surface of the perfectly luminous full moon,
one should contemplate the five-pronged vajra wisdom scepter,
gradually extending it until it pervades and encompasses the entire dharmadhātu.
With pure radiance, they illuminate the entire realm of sentient beings;
the adventitious afflictions of self and others are purified,
becoming equal and equal in their single, identical nature.
Having performed this visualization, one recites the mantra:
Oṃ tiṣṭha vajra. One should contemplate this for a long time, and then gradually withdraw the vajra.
Visualizing it as being the size of one's own body, recite the mantra:
Oṃ vajratama kuhuṃ. Then, visualize this vajra transforming into the body of the Great Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
His radiance is as bright and pure as the moon palace;
he is adorned with the crowns of the five Buddhas, celestial robes, and jeweled necklaces.
His back is against a moon disc,
with a white lotus king serving as his seat;
his right hand holds a five-pronged vajra of bodhicitta.
Press [the bell] against the heart;
with the right hand, hold the vajra-bell of the Prajñāpāramitā and press it against the hip.
One causes all the primary and secondary marks to be fully perfected.
Having performed this contemplation, one further reflects:
"All sentient beings possess the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha."
Because the body of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva pervades all things, I am non-dual and inseparable from Samantabhadra and all sentient beings.
Having observed this with precise discernment, recite the mantra seven times. The mantra is as follows:
Recite the mantra: Oṃ samantabhadra hūṃ. Having recited the mantra, one then binds the Samaya-mudrā of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra:
with both hands, interlace the fingers outwardly and clench them into fists.
Join the two middle fingers upright to form [the mudrā].
Seal the heart with this mudrā and recite [the mantra] once.
Next, place it on the forehead, then at the throat and the crown of the head, reciting the mantra once for each. The mantra is as follows:
Oṃ samayas tvaṃ. Next, one should form the mudrā of the five-buddha crown:
with both hands in the vajra-bind, extend the two middle fingers and bend their upper joints.
With the heads [of the hands] touching,
the two index fingers each grasp the upper joint of the middle fingers;
place the mudrā upon the crown of the head.
Recite the mantra once.
Next, place it at the hairline on the forehead and recite it once.
Then, move it to the right side of the crown, the back of the crown, and the left side of the crown.
Each recites the mantra once:
Oṃ sarvatathāgataraśmisaṃspharaṇa hūṃ. Next, perform the jewel-garland mudrā.
Form vajra-fists with both hands;
wrap them around each other above the forehead in the manner of tying a garland.
Then, one parts the fists behind the head as if tying a sash;
the two hands then gradually open downward from the little fingers.
Rotate the fists as if dancing.
While binding [the armor], recite the mantra:
Oṃ vajramālabhiścaya maṃ vaṃ. Next, form the Vajra Armor Mudrā.
Place both vajra fists directly at the heart;
extend the index fingers of each hand and intertwine them with one another,
while reciting the two-syllable mantra *Oṃ Cchin*.
Next, it moves to the back, again encircling it.
It returns to the navel, then to the right knee and left knee, then the navel, then the waist, then the heart, the right shoulder, the left shoulder, the throat, and finally the back of the neck.
They all wind and coil around one another;
next, they reach the forehead and the back of the head,
all forming the appearance of a bound garland or ribbon.
The two hands are slowly opened wide on both sides,
and then the palms are clapped three times;
this is called "Delighting All the Holy Multitudes."
Then recite the mantra three times. The mantra is:
Oṃ vajraduḥśaya hūṃ. Once the practitioner has manifested the body of the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, [he should proceed].
Furthermore, one should bind the Samādhi-mudrā of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and cultivate the practices and vows of Samantabhadra.
One should enter the three gates of liberation of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva’s Prajñāpāramitā.
This refers to entering the samādhi of emptiness:
directing the mind throughout the entire dharma-realm,
where suddenly not a single dharma can be apprehended.
In a brief moment, he clarified his mind and entered meditative absorption,
abiding in this gateway of contemplation;
by entering this samādhi, he eliminated all views.
To eliminate attachment to emptiness, one enters the samādhi of signlessness.
Abiding in this gateway of contemplation for a brief moment,
by entering this samādhi, one extinguishes the characteristic of emptiness.
Then one enters the samādhi of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
Within the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā*), there is fundamentally no seeking or wishing.
Having dwelt in this contemplation for a brief moment, [one proceeds].
Then, within one's own body, at the center of the chest,
one should contemplate a sphere of luminosity about the size of one cubit,
as clear and pure as the radiance of the autumn moon.
Visualizing this in the heart,
one recites the mantra of the dhāraṇī of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva as follows: *tadyathā ānaṃde naṃdapaṭe naṃda*.

khaṭi saṃgha-gaṇe-jñā-sani dharmaparicchedi asaṃkhya-padagati tīrthātavai.
saṃgha-ga-tu-ḍri-ya-pramṛṣṭe (pronounced with a retroflex *ṛ* for *pramṛṣṭe*) 16.

Sarvasattvarutakośalīyanudgate sakhavikṛtite anuvrate vrate vātarisvāhā.
Having recited the *hā*, one should immediately arrange the syllables of this dhāraṇī in a clockwise sequence upon the surface of the moon-disc of the heart,
visualizing each individual syllable as being like gold in color.
From each and every syllable, rays of light stream forth,
universally illuminating all infinite and boundless worlds.
After a long while, apply the mind with focused attention.
When the mind is undistracted, one contemplates the gateway to the meaning of the true reality within each individual syllable;
furthermore, within each and every syllable, there is the gateway to the meaning of the syllable A.

It elucidates that all phenomena are fundamentally neither born nor extinguished, neither existent nor non-existent, neither identical nor different, neither increasing nor decreasing, and neither pure nor impure.
If one can awaken to this gateway of dependent origination, which is the true nature of reality, [one will realize it].
Then one will be able to realize immeasurable and boundless samādhis and immeasurable and boundless prajñāpāramitā.
Next, one should focus the mind and contemplate.
Upon the tip of the tongue there is an eight-petaled lotus flower;
upon the flower sits a Buddha in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka), as if in meditative concentration (samādhi).
Visualize that each and every word of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* issues from the Buddha’s mouth, all appearing golden in color,
endowed with radiance, and filling the entirety of space.
One should imagine that each and every syllable transforms into the body of a Buddha,
filling the void and surrounding the reciter of the sutra.
That reciter of the sutra, according to his own capacity, [should visualize this].
One may recite a single chapter or the entire scripture,
neither too slowly nor too quickly.
When performing this contemplation, one gradually perceives that body and mind become light, peaceful, harmonious, and refreshed.
If one can long practice such contemplation,
then within meditative concentration,
one will clearly perceive all Tathāgatas expounding the profound Dharma.
Having heard this, one contemplates it and thereby enters the contemplation of the Dharmakāya Tathatā;
with a single object and a single characteristic, it is equal and uniform like empty space.
If one can practice with focused and uninterrupted cultivation,
one will enter the first bhūmi in this very life,
suddenly accumulating the provisions of merit and wisdom for one great asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
By virtue of being sustained by the empowerment of numerous Tathāgatas,
one attains the ten stages, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment, endowed with sarvajñā (omniscience),
wherein self and others are equal.
Sharing the same dharma-body as all Tathāgatas,
he constantly benefits and brings happiness to boundless sentient beings through unconditional great compassion.
Perform the great Buddha-activity.
Once the recitation and the wisdom of contemplation are completed, form the Samaya-mudrā of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and recite the mantra seven or three times.
Next, form the mudrās for the five kinds of offerings;
recite the mantras three times for each to make offerings to all the Buddhas and the assembly of noble ones.
Then, take the argha from the left side,
hold it before your forehead,
and offer it while praying for the fulfillment of your heart’s aspirations and the vast vow to attain Buddhahood.
Next, bind the seal of the Noble Acala;
turning to the left, dissolve the boundary,
thereby entering into objectless great compassion.
When self and others are equal like space,
one enters the contemplation of the Dharmakāya;
being without form or color, there is no conceptual proliferation regarding names or meanings.
Then, form the samaya-mudrā,
place it upon the crown of the head, recite the mantra once,
and bid farewell to the assembly of holy ones.
Although one performs the ritual of dismissal according to the procedures of the Mantra-gate,
one should constantly contemplate that all the assembly of noble ones is of one and the same Dharma-realm.
When the power of aspiration for neither coming nor going is fulfilled, one shall be at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Then, rising up, one should universally prostrate to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
placing the right knee upon the ground, one should recite the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna* once.
Then, one should rise and circumambulate the stūpa,
or practice walking meditation;
throughout the four modes of deportment, the mind should remain fixed upon the gateway of the contemplation of the letter A.
Entering the gate of the Prajñāpāramitā of the ultimate true reality,
in every thought-moment they universally take as their object all sentient beings within the three realms,
the six destinies, and the four modes of birth.
May I obtain the King of Sutras, the Lotus Sutra;
through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation, may I swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
